/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern async-queue
 * @options 0cff67cff6de405c
 */

/**
 * The counters, read together.
 *
 * One value rather than several getters, so that what is logged or asserted is
 * a coherent picture of one instant. Reading them separately invites a report
 * in which the numbers do not add up because something moved in between.
 *
 * `idle` is derived rather than tracked. A second source of truth for the same
 * fact is a second thing that can be wrong, and this one is the fact `onIdle`
 * resolves on.
 */
export interface OrderQueueSnapshot {
  /** How many run at once. Fixed for the life of the instance. */
  readonly concurrency: number;
  readonly running: number;
  /** Submitted and not yet started. */
  readonly pending: number;
  readonly idle: boolean;
}

/**
 * One submission waiting to start.
 *
 * `sequence` is the tie-break, and it is the reason equal priorities keep their
 * arrival order. Ordering on priority alone would leave ties to whatever the
 * insertion happens to do with equal elements — which today would be the right
 * thing, since sorting has been required to be stable since ES2019, but a queue
 * resting on a property it never states is one rewrite away from reordering
 * work silently.
 *
 * `start` is a closure rather than the task itself, because it carries the
 * halves of the caller's promise with it. That is the whole mechanism: the
 * backlog is a list of things that will settle a promise somebody else is
 * holding.
 */
interface OrderQueueEntry {
  readonly priority: number;
  /** Submission order, ascending. Breaks ties within a priority. */
  readonly sequence: number;
  readonly start: () => void;
}

/**
 * Work submitted to be run a few at a time.
 *
 * Distinct from a semaphore in one respect that decides everything else: the
 * queue holds the work rather than gating work the caller has already started.
 * That is what makes a bounded backlog, a drain signal and ordering expressible
 * here and not there.
 */
export class OrderQueue {
  readonly #concurrency: number;
  readonly #onError: (error: unknown) => void;
  readonly #backlog: OrderQueueEntry[] = [];
  #running = 0;
  #sequence = 0;
  #idleWaiters: (() => void)[] = [];

  /**
   * How many tasks run at once, and how much may wait.
   *
   * Validated rather than trusted, because these usually come from
   * configuration and both failures are silent: a concurrency of zero starts
   * nothing and presents as a hang, while a fraction makes every comparison
   * against it behave in a way nobody predicted.
   *
   * The handler is required, not optional. It is the only place a discarded
   * failure can be seen, and a queue that accepted work while having nowhere to
   * report its errors would lose them.
   */
  constructor(concurrency: number, onError: (error: unknown) => void) {
    if (!Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency < 1) {
      throw new RangeError(
        `concurrency must be a positive integer, received ${String(concurrency)}`,
      );
    }

    this.#concurrency = concurrency;
    this.#onError = onError;
  }

  /**
   * What the queue looks like right now.
   */
  snapshot(): OrderQueueSnapshot {
    return {
      concurrency: this.#concurrency,
      running: this.#running,
      pending: this.#backlog.length,
      idle: this.#running === 0 && this.#backlog.length === 0,
    };
  }

  /**
   * Submits one task, and returns it however it ends.
   *
   * The task is not called here. It is called when a worker is free, which is
   * what separates this from running everything at once and limiting it
   * afterwards: nothing the task holds is allocated until it starts, so a
   * backlog of a million submissions costs a million closures rather than a
   * million open connections.
   *
   * Higher priorities start first, and equal priorities start in submission
   * order. Note the cost of ordering strictly: low-priority work waits for as
   * long as higher-priority work keeps arriving, which under sustained load is
   * forever.
   *
   * Failures reach the handler given at construction as well as this promise,
   * so discarding it is safe. A caller who awaits it sees the error too — the
   * handler observes every failure, it does not intercept them.
   */
  run<T>(task: () => Promise<T> | T, priority = 0): Promise<T> {
    const settled = new Promise<T>((resolve, reject) => {
      const entry: OrderQueueEntry = {
        priority,
        sequence: this.#sequence++,
        start: () => {
          this.#running += 1;

          // The caller's promise and the bookkeeping are settled from the same
          // place, so the task's own promise is always handled and the queue
          // never manufactures an unhandled rejection of its own.
          void (async () => {
            try {
              resolve(await task());
            } catch (error) {
              reject(error);
            } finally {
              this.#running -= 1;
              this.#pump();
            }
          })();
        },
      };

      this.#admit(entry);
      this.#pump();
    });

    // Both halves of the sink contract, in two lines: every failure is reported
    // exactly once here, and attaching this handler is what marks `settled` as
    // handled — which is why discarding it does not take the process down.
    settled.catch((error: unknown) => {
      this.#onError(error);
    });

    return settled;
  }

  /**
   * Resolves when nothing is running and nothing is waiting.
   *
   * Never rejects, whatever the tasks did. A drain signal that failed with the
   * first failing task would make "wait for the work to finish" and "check the
   * work succeeded" the same call, and a caller wanting the first would have to
   * swallow the second.
   *
   * It answers about the work submitted so far. A task that submits more after
   * awaiting something has, for that moment, left the queue genuinely empty,
   * and no queue can wait for work it has not been told about.
   */
  onIdle(): Promise<void> {
    if (this.#running === 0 && this.#backlog.length === 0)
      return Promise.resolve();

    return new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      this.#idleWaiters.push(resolve);
    });
  }

  /**
   * Inserts one submission at its place in the order.
   *
   * Ordered by priority descending, then by sequence ascending. A binary search
   * rather than a sort per submission, which makes admission logarithmic
   * instead of linearithmic — worth having because the backlog is exactly the
   * thing that gets long.
   *
   * The sequence comparison is what keeps equal priorities in arrival order,
   * and it is written out rather than left to the insertion's treatment of
   * equal elements. See the note on the entry type for why that matters more
   * than it appears to.
   */
  #admit(entry: OrderQueueEntry): void {
    let low = 0;
    let high = this.#backlog.length;

    while (low < high) {
      const middle = (low + high) >>> 1;
      const at = this.#backlog[middle];
      if (at === undefined) break;

      const ahead =
        at.priority > entry.priority ||
        (at.priority === entry.priority && at.sequence < entry.sequence);

      if (ahead) low = middle + 1;
      else high = middle;
    }

    this.#backlog.splice(low, 0, entry);
  }

  /**
   * Starts whatever the free workers can take, then announces what that
   * changed.
   *
   * Called after every change to either counter, and the only place the two
   * signals are resolved from. Announcing them where the counters change
   * instead would mean four places that each have to remember to, which is
   * three more than can be checked by reading one method.
   */
  #pump(): void {
    while (this.#running < this.#concurrency && this.#backlog.length > 0) {
      const next = this.#backlog.shift();
      if (next === undefined) break;

      next.start();
    }

    if (this.#running === 0 && this.#backlog.length === 0) {
      const waiting = this.#idleWaiters;
      this.#idleWaiters = [];
      for (const resolve of waiting) resolve();
    }
  }
}

## order-queue-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern async-queue
 * @options 0cff67cff6de405c
 */

/**
 * Indexing a stream of files without reading them all into memory first.
 *
 * The case a queue is for and a semaphore is not: the work arrives over time
 * rather than as a list, so there is nothing to `map` over, and the producer is
 * faster than the workers.
 */

import { OrderQueue } from "./order-queue.js";

/**
 * Indexes every file, a few at a time, and returns once the last has finished.
 *
 * Note what this does not bound: the loop submits as fast as it can read, so on
 * a large stream the backlog is the memory ceiling. A bounded rendering of this
 * pattern is the answer where the producer is faster than the workers.
 *
 * Nothing awaits an individual submission, which is only safe because failures
 * have somewhere to go. Under the promise rendering the same loop would end the
 * process on the first failing file.
 *
 * `onIdle` is the wait, rather than keeping the promises and awaiting them
 * together: the list of outstanding work is what the queue is already for.
 */
export async function indexAll(
  files: AsyncIterable<string>,
  index: (path: string) => Promise<void>,
  concurrency: number,
  report: (error: unknown) => void,
): Promise<void> {
  const queue = new OrderQueue(concurrency, report);

  for await (const path of files) {
    void queue.run(async () => await index(path), path.endsWith(".md") ? 1 : 0);
  }

  await queue.onIdle();
}

/**
 * What the queue is doing, for whatever reports on it.
 *
 * `pending` is the number worth watching. Work arriving faster than it drains
 * means the concurrency is now the bottleneck, and it is the difference between
 * a system that is busy and one that is falling behind.
 */
export function describeLoad(queue: OrderQueue): string {
  const { running, concurrency, pending } = queue.snapshot();
  return `${String(running)}/${String(concurrency)} indexing, ${String(pending)} waiting`;
}
```
